[![Image 1: An over-the-counter stablecoin exchange](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/cf/Over-the-counter-crypto-exchange.jpeg/250px-Over-the-counter-crypto-exchange.jpeg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Over-the-counter-crypto-exchange.jpeg)

An [over-the-counter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Over-the-counter_(finance) "Over-the-counter (finance)") stablecoin exchange in [Hong Kong](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hong_Kong "Hong Kong")

A **stablecoin** is a type of [cryptocurrency](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cryptocurrency "Cryptocurrency") that aims to maintain a stable value relative to a specified asset, a pool or basket of assets. The specified asset might refer to [fiat currency](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fiat_money "Fiat money"), [commodity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commodity_market "Commodity market"), or other cryptocurrencies.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stablecoin#cite_note-Bank_of_England-2023-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stablecoin#cite_note-2) Despite the name, stablecoins are not necessarily stable. Stablecoins rely on stabilization tools such as reserve assets or [algorithms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algorithm "Algorithm") that match supply and demand to try to maintain a stable value.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stablecoin#cite_note-Adachi-2022-3)

Historically, multiple stablecoins have failed to maintain their value relative to the underlying assets. With a growing number of market transactions involving stablecoins, their issuance and usage are increasingly regulated by governments around the world.

## Background

Stablecoins emerged in 2014 as a method for investors in cryptocurrencies to park their money when they invest in other highly [volatile](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Volatility_(finance) "Volatility (finance)") cryptocurrencies.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stablecoin#cite_note-Towfighi-2025-4)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stablecoin#cite_note-Dionysopoulos-2024-5) Stablecoins are now mainly used for buying or selling cryptoassets, and for making cross-border payments.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stablecoin#cite_note-Bank_of_England-2023-1) According to the [Bank for International Settlements](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bank_for_International_Settlements "Bank for International Settlements") in July 2025, 90% of the market capitalization of stablecoins was either in [Tether](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tether_(cryptocurrency) "Tether (cryptocurrency)") or [USDC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/USDC_(cryptocurrency) "USDC (cryptocurrency)").[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stablecoin#cite_note-Aldasoro-2025-6):4 According to the [Financial Action Task Force](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Financial_Action_Task_Force "Financial Action Task Force"), the market capitalization of stablecoins reached $316 billion in October 2025, while daily trading volume reached $156 billion. Within the stablecoin market, 95% of them are backed by fiat currency, while 97% among those fiat currency-backed stablecoins are denominated in US dollar.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stablecoin#cite_note-Financial_Action_Task_Force-2024-7):11

## Types of stablecoin

[![Image 2](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/de/Stablecoin_logos_montage.svg/250px-Stablecoin_logos_montage.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Stablecoin_logos_montage.svg)

Some logos of well known stablecoins: [USDT](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tether_(cryptocurrency) "Tether (cryptocurrency)"), [DAI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dai_(cryptocurrency) "Dai (cryptocurrency)"), [USDC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/USDC_(cryptocurrency) "USDC (cryptocurrency)"), and [TerraUSD](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TerraUSD "TerraUSD")

### Fiat-backed stablecoins

Fiat-backed stablecoins are stablecoins that are backed by assets denominated in a [fiat currency](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fiat_money "Fiat money"). The value of a fiat-backed stablecoin is based on the value of the backing currency, which is supposedly held by a third party custodian. The issuer defends the peg of the stablecoin by holding mostly fiat-denominated short-term assets, such as [treasury bonds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Treasury_security "United States Treasury security"), high-quality [commercial paper](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commercial_paper "Commercial paper"), [repurchase agreements](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Repurchase_agreement "Repurchase agreement") and [bank deposits](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bank_deposits "Bank deposits"). Therefore, the structure of fiat-backed stablecoins closely resembles that of [money market funds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Money_market_fund "Money market fund") (MMFs), and they are exposed to similar risk of large-scale redemption requests causing negative contagion effects on the financial system.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stablecoin#cite_note-Aldasoro-2024-8)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stablecoin#cite_note-Adachi-2021-9)

As of October 2025, nearly 97% of fiat-backed stablecoins are pegged to the US dollar.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stablecoin#cite_note-Financial_Action_Task_Force-2024-7) Major examples of US-dollar-pegged stablecoins are [Tether](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tether_(cryptocurrency) "Tether (cryptocurrency)")'s USDT and [Circle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Circle_Internet_Group "Circle Internet Group")'s [USDC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/USDC_(cryptocurrency) "USDC (cryptocurrency)").[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stablecoin#cite_note-10) For Euro-pegged stablecoins, examples include Circle's EURC,[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stablecoin#cite_note-11) EUR Tether, and Stasis EUR.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stablecoin#cite_note-12)

### Cryptocurrency-backed stablecoins

Cryptocurrency-backed stablecoins are stablecoins using other cryptocurrencies as collateral. The reason such stablecoins are created is that by utilizing [smart contracts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smart_contract "Smart contract"), they allow a decentralized network to track the price of the US dollar as closely as possible. Another use case of cryptocurrency-backed stablecoins is to convert a cryptocurrency into [ERC20](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ERC20 "ERC20") compatible standard to enable trading on another blockchain.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stablecoin#cite_note-13)

### Commodity-backed stablecoins

Commodity-backed stablecoins are stablecoins that are backed by commodities. Examples are PAX Gold and Tether Gold.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stablecoin#cite_note-Kosse-2023-14)

### Algorithmic stablecoins

Algorithmic stablecoins, sometimes called [seigniorage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seigniorage "Seigniorage")-style stablecoin, are stablecoins with no reserve assets or only partial reserve assets. They utilize algorithms that match supply and demand of the stablecoins to maintain a stable value. The European Central Bank suggests that algorithmic stablecoins should be treated as unbacked crypto-assets.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stablecoin#cite_note-Adachi-2022-3) Some major examples of algorithmic stablecoins are Celo Dollar, [Tron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tron_(blockchain) "Tron (blockchain)")'s USDD and Kava's USDX.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stablecoin#cite_note-Krause-2025-15)

## Uses of stablecoins

### Trading other cryptocurrencies

Stablecoins provide convenience for investors in cryptocurrencies, as a simpler way to buy and sell other more volatile cryptocurrencies.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stablecoin#cite_note-Adachi-2022-3)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stablecoin#cite_note-Towfighi-2025-4)_[Planet Money](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Planet\_Money "Planet Money")_ has described this use of stablecoins as similar to [casino chips](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Casino_chips "Casino chips"), as they simplify buying and selling other cryptocurrencies before eventually being traded for money.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stablecoin#cite_note-16)

### Cross-border payments

According to a 2025 report from the [International Monetary Fund](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Monetary_Fund "International Monetary Fund") (IMF), cross-border flows of stablecoin surpassed those of unbacked crypto assets in early 2022. According to the IMF, Asia and the Pacific region have the most stablecoin activity, while after adjusting for [GDP](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GDP "GDP"), the majority of stablecoins flow from North America to other locations. The report estimated that stablecoin cross-border flow was $1.4 trillion dollars in 2024, compared to the global cross-border payment market of approximately one quadrillion dollars. In [advanced economies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Developed_country "Developed country"), cross-border flows is dominated by traditional [payment systems](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Payment_system "Payment system"). The largest share of stablecoins being used for cross-border transactions was among emerging markets and [developing economies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Developing_country "Developing country").[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stablecoin#cite_note-IMF-2025-17)

According to a study by the [University of Cambridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Cambridge_Judge_Business_School "University of Cambridge Judge Business School"), the most cited reason for using stablecoins in cross-border settlement is the 24/7 settlement capability, allowing transactions to take place outside banking hours.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stablecoin#cite_note-18) A 2025 study in the journal _Telematics and Informatics_, of 866 U.S.-based adults who had sent remittances within the previous year, 26% reported using stablecoins for cross-border transfers, with 34% also using other methods.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stablecoin#cite_note-Ante2025-19)

### Currency substitution

According to [Chainalysis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chainalysis "Chainalysis"), due to the volatility of the Venezuelan bolivar, some Venezuelans use US dollar-denominated stablecoins to preserve value and transact in a more stable currency.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stablecoin#cite_note-20) In January 2026, it was reported that US dollar-denominated stablecoins are increasingly being used in domestic transactions in Venezuela due to prolonged period of [hyperinflation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hyperinflation_in_Venezuela "Hyperinflation in Venezuela"), [sanctions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sanctions_during_the_Venezuelan_crisis "Sanctions during the Venezuelan crisis"), and [capital controls](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capital_control "Capital control").[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stablecoin#cite_note-21)

A report by [Standard Chartered](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Standard_Chartered "Standard Chartered") warned that the prevalence of US dollar-denominated stablecoins could potentially cause $1 trillion from developing countries to flow to stablecoins, causing loss of [bank deposits](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bank_deposits "Bank deposits"). The capital outflow would be caused by risk aversion of individuals within the developing countries against sudden sharp [currency depreciation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Currency_depreciation "Currency depreciation").[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stablecoin#cite_note-22)

### Aid distribution

Since 2019, Oxfam began distributing humanitarian aid to residents of [Vanuatu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vanuatu "Vanuatu") using US dollar stablecoins. By 2022, the project registered 35,000 people in the Pacific region and has distributed aid of around $2 million to participants.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stablecoin#cite_note-23)

According to a report published by the [United Nations Development Programme](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Nations_Development_Programme "United Nations Development Programme") (UNDP) in January 2026, the UNDP is running pilot programmes involving stablecoins in Columbia, Syria, Gambia, Papua New Guinea, Kazakhstan, and Morocco. For example, in Syria, the UNDP Cash-for-Work programmes experienced difficulty delivering stipends to Syrians due to lack of financial infrastructure, and so the UNDP is experimenting with sending stablecoins to the beneficiaries instead.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stablecoin#cite_note-24)

According to media report in 2021, Portuguese nonprofit ImpactMarket reported distributing over $1 million in Celo Dollar stablecoins to more than 18,000 beneficiaries in 102 locations in Africa, and said some local merchants had begun accepting the tokens for payments.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stablecoin#cite_note-25)

## Policy and regulatory issues

### Money laundering and terrorism financing

In January 2024, the [United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Nations_Office_on_Drugs_and_Crime "United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime") (UNODC) reported that stablecoins, particularly USDT, had become the cryptocurrency of choice for organized crime groups engaged in cyberfraud and money laundering in East and Southeast Asia.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stablecoin#cite_note-26)

Reuters reported in 2023 that groups designated as terrorist organizations by Israel, the United States and other countries were using stablecoins on the Tron blockchain instead of more volatile bitcoin tokens to preserve the value of transferred funds.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stablecoin#cite_note-27)

The intergovernmental [Financial Action Task Force](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Financial_Action_Task_Force "Financial Action Task Force") (FATF) has reported that stablecoins are increasingly used for illicit financial activity, including money laundering, terrorism financing, sanctions evasion, and proliferation financing. The report states that stablecoins such as USDT (Tether) and USDC (Circle) provide a relatively stable medium for moving proceeds compared with more volatile cryptocurrencies, and that their liquidity, interoperability, and ease of cross-border transfer make them attractive for illicit use.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stablecoin#cite_note-Financial_Action_Task_Force-2024-7)

### Erosion of monetary sovereignty

After the passing of the [GENIUS Act](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GENIUS_Act "GENIUS Act") by the Trump administration in the United States, Jürgen Schaaf, adviser to the [European Central Bank](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Central_Bank "European Central Bank") (ECB) wrote that widespread adoption of US dollar stablecoins could erode European [monetary sovereignty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monetary_sovereignty "Monetary sovereignty") and [financial stability](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Financial_stability "Financial stability").[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stablecoin#cite_note-28) Scholars in China and Singapore have both described the GENIUS Act as a strategic move to increase demand for US Treasuries and therefore an attempt to consolidate the hegemony of the US dollar.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stablecoin#cite_note-29)[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stablecoin#cite_note-30)[Lesetja Kganyago](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lesetja_Kganyago "Lesetja Kganyago"), Governor of [South African Reserve Bank](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_African_Reserve_Bank "South African Reserve Bank"), expressed that US dollar stablecoins are being used to undermine African currencies, and is concerned that some African countries might lose their monetary sovereignty.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stablecoin#cite_note-31)[Agnès Bénassy-Quéré](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agn%C3%A8s_B%C3%A9nassy-Qu%C3%A9r%C3%A9 "Agnès Bénassy-Quéré"), Deputy Governor of the [Banque de France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bank_of_France "Bank of France"), and [François Villeroy de Galhau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fran%C3%A7ois_Villeroy_de_Galhau "François Villeroy de Galhau"), Governor of the Banque de France, warned that Europe's monetary sovereignty is threatened by US dollar-denominated stablecoins.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stablecoin#cite_note-32)

In March 2026, a research published by the ECB examined the effect of foreign-currency-denominated stablecoins on the monetary sovereignty of Europe. The adoption of US dollar-denominated stablecoins would import foreign [monetary policies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monetary_policy "Monetary policy") into Europe, weakening the ability of central banks to affect short-term interest rates, complicate liquidity management within the banking system, and increase exchange-rate-related volatility in funding flows. In extreme cases, it could make Europe's own monetary policy tools ineffective.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stablecoin#cite_note-33)

### Sanction avoidance

In response to [sanctions against Russian entities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sanctions_involving_Russia "Sanctions involving Russia"), A7A5, a rouble-pegged stablecoin, was launched by [Promsvyazbank](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Promsvyazbank "Promsvyazbank") and Moldovan oligarch [Ilan Șor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ilan_Shor "Ilan Shor"). The stablecoin was used by Russian businesses to conduct cross-border payments and by the Russian state to carry out an [influence campaign](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Disinformation_in_the_Russian_invasion_of_Ukraine "Disinformation in the Russian invasion of Ukraine").[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stablecoin#cite_note-34)[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stablecoin#cite_note-35)[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stablecoin#cite_note-36)

In October 2025, the UN's Multilateral Sanctions Monitoring Team found that [North Korea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Korea "North Korea") avoided [sanctions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sanctions_against_North_Korea "Sanctions against North Korea") by using stablecoin for sale and transfer of military equipment and raw materials.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stablecoin#cite_note-37) The report alleged that North Korean officials sold military-grade satellite communications systems to a buyer in [Laos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laos "Laos") and a [portable air defense system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Air_defense_system "Air defense system") to a buyer in [Sudan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sudan "Sudan"). In both cases the buyers paid in USDT.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stablecoin#cite_note-38) In January 2026, it was reported that the [Central Bank of Iran](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_Bank_of_Iran "Central Bank of Iran") is accumulating stablecoins while facing [sanctions against the Iranian regime](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_sanctions_against_Iran "International sanctions against Iran").[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stablecoin#cite_note-39)

In November 2025, the [Australian government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Department_of_Foreign_Affairs_and_Trade_(Australia) "Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade (Australia)") published an advisory note saying that terrorist group [ISIL](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Islamic_State "Islamic State") prefers using USDT for fundraising and to circumvent sanctions.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stablecoin#cite_note-40)

## Financial risks and stability concerns

### De-pegging risk

While stablecoins aim to maintain the peg with underlying assets, they are constantly traded on the market and therefore subject to market volatility. A stablecoin can deviate from the peg due to a number of reasons, such as liquidity stress, increase in market demand, mismanagement of reserves, fluctuations in prices of other cryptocurrencies, design flaws of stabilization mechanic, etc.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stablecoin#cite_note-41)[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stablecoin#cite_note-42)[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stablecoin#cite_note-43)

### Contagion risk on financial market

Since fiat-backed stablecoins are structurally similar to money market funds, they pose similar contagion risk, in which a large amount of redemption caused the selling of underlying assets, further pushing down the price of the underlying assets and creating more demand for redemption.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stablecoin#cite_note-Aldasoro-2024-8)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stablecoin#cite_note-Adachi-2021-9)

Partner banks of stablecoin issuers would also face substantial increase in liquidity risk exposure due to linkage with fiat-backed stablecoins. Unlike money market funds, stablecoins are designed to be settlement instruments, and therefore may face more rapid conversion, resulting in increased liquidity risk.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stablecoin#cite_note-44)

### Counterparty risk

Reserve-backed stablecoins require a third party custodian to hold the reserve assets to maintain price stability. The concentration of reserve deposits creates a counterparty risk in which the custodian may fail in the case of a [bank run](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bank_run "Bank run"). In March 2023, the price of Circle's USDC de-pegged temporarily during the [banking crisis in the United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_United_States_banking_crisis "2023 United States banking crisis") in which [Signature Bank](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Signature_Bank "Signature Bank"), [Silvergate Bank](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silvergate_Bank "Silvergate Bank"), and [Silicon Valley Bank](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Collapse_of_Silicon_Valley_Bank "Collapse of Silicon Valley Bank") collapsed.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stablecoin#cite_note-45)

### Solvency risk

Fiat-backed stablecoins maintain the peg with underlying currency by using reserve assets such as [US Treasuries](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Treasury_security "United States Treasury security"). Since the value of Treasuries are affected by interest rate, it is possible for stablecoins to become insolvent when interest rate increase. Some stablecoin issuers mitigate this risk by allocating the majority of their backing asset into short duration securities which are less affected by interest rate.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stablecoin#cite_note-:0-46)

### Technology risk

In an analysis on IMF's [Finance & Development](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Finance_&_Development "Finance & Development"), Professor [Hélène Rey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H%C3%A9l%C3%A8ne_Rey "Hélène Rey") wrote that advancement in [quantum computing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quantum_computing "Quantum computing") is often ignored in the discussion of stablecoins. Quantum computers in the near future may be able to break [public-key cryptography](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Public-key_cryptography "Public-key cryptography"), allowing hackers to attack the currency networks used by stablecoins, potentially causing financial crises.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stablecoin#cite_note-47)

A research by the [Massachusetts Institute of Technology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Massachusetts_Institute_of_Technology "Massachusetts Institute of Technology") pointed out that flaws in the logic of [smart contracts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smart_contract "Smart contract") could potentially result in stablecoin issuers losing control of the supply of stablecoins and their network. Cross-chain bridges are another [attack vector](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Attack_vector "Attack vector") which can cause deposit and redemption issues.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stablecoin#cite_note-:0-46)

### Lack of reserve transparency

[Tether's USDT](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tether_(cryptocurrency) "Tether (cryptocurrency)") is currently the world's largest [market capitalization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Market_capitalization "Market capitalization") stablecoin. Tether initially claimed their stablecoin is fully backed by fiat currency. However, in October 2021, it failed to produce audits for reserves used to collateralize the quantity of minted USDT stablecoin.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stablecoin#cite_note-48) Tether were fined $41 million by the [Commodity Futures Trading Commission](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commodity_Futures_Trading_Commission "Commodity Futures Trading Commission") (CFTC) for deceiving consumers.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stablecoin#cite_note-49) The CFTC found that Tether only had enough fiat reserves to guarantee their stablecoin for 27.6% of the time during 2016 to 2018. Since then, Tether began issuing assurance reports on USDT backing, although some speculation persists regarding the use of Chinese commercial paper for reserves.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stablecoin#cite_note-50) As at February 2026, Tether had never completed an [audit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Audit "Audit") by an accounting firm.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stablecoin#cite_note-51)

### Fragmentation of liquidity

[Hyun-Song Shin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hyun-Song_Shin "Hyun-Song Shin"), governor of the [Bank of Korea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bank_of_Korea "Bank of Korea"), wrote in his research that since stablecoins on different blockchains are not interoperable, they create a fragmented ecosystem as compared to fiat money, which has the advantage of [network effect](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Network_effect "Network effect"). The requirement of "gas fee" for transactions, and the increase in fee when traffic is high, creates a dilemma in which users are incentivized to switch to blockchains with lower fees, ensuring that the ecosystem is fragmented.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stablecoin#cite_note-52)

### "Death spiral" of algorithmic stablecoin

Algorithmic stablecoins are vulnerable to a de-pegging process known as "death spiral",[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stablecoin#cite_note-53)[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stablecoin#cite_note-54) in which an external event, such as the tightening of global liquidity, led to heavy redemption of the stablecoin. This triggered the minting of the linked token to burn the stablecoin, causing the supply of the linked token to increase exponentially, further causing a decrease in price.[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stablecoin#cite_note-55)[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stablecoin#cite_note-Briola-2023-56)

A famous case of death spiral is the [TerraUSD](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TerraUSD "TerraUSD") (UST), which was created by [Terraform Labs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Terraform_Labs "Terraform Labs") founded by [Do Kwon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Do_Kwon "Do Kwon"). TerraUSD was meant to maintain a 1:1 peg with the United States dollar.[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stablecoin#cite_note-cnbc-57) Instead of being backed by dollars, UST was designed to keep its peg by linking it with another Terra network token, LUNA. The mechanism worked by providing an economic incentive for [arbitrage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arbitrage "Arbitrage"). If UST lost its peg and traded below $1, an arbitrager could purchase it on the secondary market and redeem it for $1 worth of LUNA. Correspondingly, if UST traded higher than $1, market actors could mint new UST by locking in $1 of LUNA and then sell the new UST on the market for a profit. However, this mechanism assumes there is sufficient market demand for UST and LUNA, making the stablecoin inherently fragile.[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stablecoin#cite_note-58)

In May 2022, UST broke its peg with its price plunging to 10 cents,[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stablecoin#cite_note-59) while LUNA fell to "virtually zero", down from an all-time high of $119.51.[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stablecoin#cite_note-60) The collapse wiped out almost $45 billion of [market capitalization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Market_capitalization "Market capitalization") over the course of a week.[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stablecoin#cite_note-61)[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stablecoin#cite_note-wired20220512-62)

In the case of TerraUSD, another contributing factor to its failure was its [proof-of-stake](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proof_of_stake "Proof of stake") mechanism. The fall in the price of LUNA caused validators to sell their stakes, allowing malign actors to become dominant validators.[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stablecoin#cite_note-63)

## Comparison between Stablecoin and CBDC

A stablecoin should not be confused with a [central bank digital currency](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_bank_digital_currency "Central bank digital currency") (CBDC). CBDC is issued by [central banks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_bank "Central bank"), meaning that they are a direct claim on the central bank, while stablecoin is issued by private entity.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stablecoin#cite_note-Bank_of_England-2023-1)[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stablecoin#cite_note-64)

Another difference is that CBDC, being issued by central banks, would belong to the [monetary base](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monetary_base "Monetary base") (M0),[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stablecoin#cite_note-65) while stablecoins issued by commercial financial institutions would belong to the [monetary aggregate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/M2_monetary_aggregate "M2 monetary aggregate") (M2).[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stablecoin#cite_note-66)

The European Central Bank's [digital euro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Digital_euro "Digital euro") project has been under consideration since 2021 but has not been legislated by the [European Parliament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Parliament "European Parliament") as of August 2025. [Christine Lagarde](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christine_Lagarde "Christine Lagarde"), president of European Central Bank, called it a "strategic priority" for Europe in response to US legislation of stablecoins.[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stablecoin#cite_note-67)

## Stablecoin and interest return

While most stablecoins are non-interest bearing and therefore do not provide [interest returns](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interest "Interest") to the holder, some issuers and service providers began offering yield-bearing stablecoins in an attempt to gain market share.[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stablecoin#cite_note-68)[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stablecoin#cite_note-69)[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stablecoin#cite_note-70)[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stablecoin#cite_note-71)

The reason most stablecoins with centralized issuers do not provide interest return is because that would potentially make them [financial securities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Security_(finance) "Security (finance)"), thus falling under regulatory regime. The US's _GENIUS Act_, Europe's _MiCAR_, and Hong Kong's _Stablecoin Bill_ all explicitly prohibit the provision of yield-bearing stablecoins by regulated issuers.[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stablecoin#cite_note-72)[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stablecoin#cite_note-73)[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stablecoin#cite_note-74) Australian regulator treats yield-bearing stablecoins as managed investment schemes.[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stablecoin#cite_note-Australian_Securities_and_Investments_Commission-2025-75) In February 2026, media reported that legislation in the US regarding the provision of interest was stalled due to opposition from banks.[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stablecoin#cite_note-76)

### Yield provided by cryptoasset service providers

Some cryptoasset service providers (CASPs) such as [trading platforms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electronic_trading_platform "Electronic trading platform") and [market makers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Market_maker "Market maker") developed products for stablecoin users to earn interests. For example, a user can buy stablecoins through a trading platform and re-lend the bought stablecoins to the platform. The platform then provides the stablecoins to institutional borrowers to earn interest. The interest is passed to the user after subtracting the platform's margin. The European Union and Hong Kong completely prohibit CASPs from offering yield on payment stablecoins, while Singapore restricted such products to institutional investors under limited conditions.[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stablecoin#cite_note-77)

### Yield farming in decentralized platform

While issuers may not directly provide interest return, [decentralized financial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Decentralized_finance "Decentralized finance") platforms are another possible avenue for earning interests. By providing stablecoins for liquidity on decentralized platforms, holders of stablecoins can get a share of the fees paid by liquidity takers. This process is known as "yield farming".[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stablecoin#cite_note-78)

Contrary to popular belief, yield farming is not risk free, because the holders are engaged in lending activity. In the case of the TerraUSD, initially to drive adoption, the Anchor protocol was created to offer a yield of 19.5% to depositors of the stablecoin, a rate much higher than the return on US Treasuries. Thus, a large amount of the stablecoin is locked in the Anchor protocol. Subsequently when the price of TerraUSD began to crash. The holders are unable to cash out of their position and are left holding the bag.[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stablecoin#cite_note-79)[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stablecoin#cite_note-Briola-2023-56)

## Legislation and regulation

### Armenia

The [Central Bank of Armenia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_Bank_of_Armenia "Central Bank of Armenia") (CBA) has adopted the _Law on Crypto Assets_ in 2025 to strengthen consumer protection in cryptocurrency transactions. In addition, the CBA is trying to introduce regulations on issuance of stablecoins in 2026 with assistance from the IMF.[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stablecoin#cite_note-80)[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stablecoin#cite_note-81)

### Australia

Stablecoins in Australia are regulated by the [Australian Securities and Investments Commission](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Australian_Securities_and_Investments_Commission "Australian Securities and Investments Commission") (ASIC). In December 2024, the ASIC published the "_Information Sheet 225 Crypto-assets_" (INFO 225), establishing the regulatory requirement of stablecoins under "_Corporations Act 2001_".[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stablecoin#cite_note-82) Under the definition, issuers of stablecoin are treated as operating non-cash payment facilities; algorithmic stablecoins are treated as derivatives; while yield-bearing stablecoins are treated as managed investment schemes.[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stablecoin#cite_note-Australian_Securities_and_Investments_Commission-2025-75) In September and December 2025, the ASIC issued exemptions to obtain licenses for intermediaries providing services related to stablecoins and distributing stablecoins.[[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stablecoin#cite_note-83)

### Bahrain

In July 2025, the [Central Bank of Bahrain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_Bank_of_Bahrain "Central Bank of Bahrain") introduced the _Stablecoin Issuance and Offering (SIO) Module_. Under the regulation, stablecoin issuers can issue single currency fiat-backed stablecoins pegged to the [Bahraini Dinar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bahraini_dinar "Bahraini dinar"), US dollar, or any other fiat currency upon obtaining approval of the central bank. Algorithmic stablecoins are prohibited.[[84]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stablecoin#cite_note-84)[[85]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stablecoin#cite_note-85)

### Canada

In November 2025, the Canadian government under [Mark Carney](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mark_Carney "Mark Carney") announced in the [Federal Budget 2025](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_Canadian_federal_budget "2025 Canadian federal budget") proposed legislation to regulate the issuance of stablecoins. The legislation is expected to require issuers to maintain asset reserves, govern redemption policies, implement risk management frameworks, and protect [personal information](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Personal_data "Personal data") of Canadians. The _Retail Payment Activities Act_ will also be amended to enable regulation of [payment service providers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Payment_service_provider "Payment service provider") using stablecoins.[[86]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stablecoin#cite_note-86) The proposed legislation was made in direct response to the United States' legislation of the _GENIUS Act_.[[87]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stablecoin#cite_note-87)

### China

Stablecoins are considered illegal in [Mainland China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mainland_China "Mainland China").[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stablecoin#cite_note-88) The [People's Bank of China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/People's_Bank_of_China "People's Bank of China"), the central bank of China, also asked Chinese companies, including [Ant Group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ant_Group "Ant Group") and [JD.com](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/JD.com "JD.com"), to stop their plans to issue stablecoins in the [Hong Kong Special Administrative Region](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hong_Kong_Special_Administrative_Region "Hong Kong Special Administrative Region") in October 2025.[[89]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stablecoin#cite_note-89) The central bank further clarified in November 2025 that stablecoins are considered non-compliant with current regulation and asked regulatory bodies and law enforcement to crackdown on the use of stablecoins.[[90]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stablecoin#cite_note-90) In February 2026, the [China Securities Regulatory Commission](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China_Securities_Regulatory_Commission "China Securities Regulatory Commission") (CSRC) issued a notice banning the issuance of Renminbi-denominated stablecoins within and outside China, the reason being that currency issuance is a matter of [sovereignty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sovereignty "Sovereignty").[[91]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stablecoin#cite_note-91)

### European Union

The [European Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Union "European Union") introduced the [_Markets in Crypto-Assets Regulation_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Markets_in_Crypto-Assets "Markets in Crypto-Assets") (MiCAR) in June 2023. The regulation became applicable to asset-referenced tokens and e-money tokens on 30 June 2024.[[92]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stablecoin#cite_note-92) MiCAR has no clear regulation on global firms issuing the same stablecoin both from an EU-regulated entity and from a third-country entity, causing concern that in that event of large scale redemption of a multi-country stablecoin, the reserves located in the EU might be quickly depleted.[[93]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stablecoin#cite_note-93) In September 2025, a consortium of nine European banks announced the planned launch of a MiCAR compliant stablecoin in response to the dominance of US denominated stablecoins on the market.[[94]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stablecoin#cite_note-94)

### Hong Kong

In December 2024, [Hong Kong](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hong_Kong "Hong Kong") gazetted its _Stablecoins Bill_.[[95]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stablecoin#cite_note-95) The bill was passed in May 2025.[[96]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stablecoin#cite_note-ReutersHK-96) The [Hong Kong Monetary Authority](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hong_Kong_Monetary_Authority "Hong Kong Monetary Authority") (HKMA), the regulatory body of stablecoins in Hong Kong, warned the public to "rein in the euphoria".[[97]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stablecoin#cite_note-97)[[96]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stablecoin#cite_note-ReutersHK-96) In particular, guidelines require stablecoin issuers to have strict rules on [anti-money laundering](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anti%E2%80%93money_laundering "Anti–money laundering"), [risk management](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Risk_management "Risk management"), and [corporate governance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corporate_governance "Corporate governance").[[98]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stablecoin#cite_note-98) In April 2026, the HKMA issued stablecoin licenses to [HSBC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HSBC_(Hong_Kong) "HSBC (Hong Kong)") and [Standard Chartered](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Standard_Chartered_Hong_Kong "Standard Chartered Hong Kong").[[99]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stablecoin#cite_note-99)

### Japan

In June 2022, Japan's [Financial Services Agency](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Financial_Services_Agency "Financial Services Agency") launched the _Regulatory Framework for Crypto-assets and Stablecoins_.[[100]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stablecoin#cite_note-100) The regulation requires stablecoin issuer of fiat-backed stablecoin (known as digital-money type stablecoins in Japan) to register with the agency. The agency views algorithmic stablecoin as crypto assets and does not require issuer to register. However, intermediaries such as crypto exchanges are subject to regulations.[[101]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stablecoin#cite_note-101) In August 2025, fintech company JPYC received approval by the agency to launch the first stablecoin pegged to the [Japanese Yen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japanese_yen "Japanese yen").[[102]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stablecoin#cite_note-102) The first yen-pegged stablecoin launched in October 2025.[[103]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stablecoin#cite_note-103)

### Kyrgyzstan

In November 2025, Kyrgyzstan launched the first national stablecoin, USDKG. The issuer is state-owned company Virtual Asset Issuer OJSC. The stablecoin is backed by gold and pegged to the US dollar.[[104]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stablecoin#cite_note-104)[[105]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stablecoin#cite_note-105)

### Russia

In September 2025, the [Central Bank of Russia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_Bank_of_Russia "Central Bank of Russia") approved the stablecoin A7A5 as a digital financial asset which can be used by Russian importers and exporters for cross-border settlements.[[106]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stablecoin#cite_note-106)

### Singapore

In November 2023, the [Monetary Authority of Singapore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monetary_Authority_of_Singapore "Monetary Authority of Singapore") finalized its _Stablecoin Regulatory Framework_ after conducting public consultation since October 2022.[[107]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stablecoin#cite_note-107) Issuers of stablecoins are required to maintain a portfolio of reserve assets denominated in the currency of the stablecoin peg.[[108]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stablecoin#cite_note-108) On 16 November 2023, the regulator approved [Paxos Digital](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paxos_Trust_Company "Paxos Trust Company") and StraitsX as stablecoin issuers.[[109]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stablecoin#cite_note-109)

### South Africa

In August 2026, the [South African Reserve Bank](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_African_Reserve_Bank "South African Reserve Bank") and [South Africa National Treasury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Treasury_(South_Africa) "National Treasury (South Africa)") proposed the _Crypto Assets Manual for cross-border activities_, which would ban corporate cross-border stablecoin transactions, and block any incoming payments from private wallets.[[110]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stablecoin#cite_note-110)

### South Korea

Regulations on the issuance of stablecoins in South Korea are being discussed. In February 2026, [Bank of Korea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bank_of_Korea "Bank of Korea"), the central bank of South Korea, suggested that only licensed [commercial banks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commercial_bank "Commercial bank") should be able to issue [won](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Korean_won "South Korean won")-denominated stablecoins to alleviate concerns regarding money laundering and financial stability.[[111]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stablecoin#cite_note-111)[[112]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stablecoin#cite_note-112) However, the [Financial Services Commission](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Financial_Services_Commission_(South_Korea) "Financial Services Commission (South Korea)") (FSC) suggested a more open approach on the participation of technology firms, arguing that a rigid approach would hinder innovation.[[113]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stablecoin#cite_note-113)

### Taiwan

In June 2026, the Taiwan's Legislative Yuan passed the _Virtual Asset Service Act_, which provides a framework for regulating all virtual assets including stablecoin. The law requires stablecoin issuers to maintain full reserve backing, with segregated reserve assets held in trust by domestic financial institutions. The reserve assets are protected from claims by other creditors if the issuer enters bankruptcy proceedings. Stablecoin iIssuers must also undergo regular audits and are prohibited from paying interest or other returns to holders.[[114]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stablecoin#cite_note-114)

### UAE

In June 2024, the [Central Bank of the UAE](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_Bank_of_the_United_Arab_Emirates "Central Bank of the United Arab Emirates") established the _Payment Token Services Regulations_ to regulate the use of stablecoins in the UAE. The regulations prohibit persons within the UAE from accepting stablecoins for the sale of goods and services except licensed payment token.[[115]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stablecoin#cite_note-115)[[116]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stablecoin#cite_note-116)In April 2025, the [sovereign wealth fund](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sovereign_wealth_fund "Sovereign wealth fund") of [Abu Dhabi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abu_Dhabi "Abu Dhabi"), ADQ, and the [First Abu Dhabi Bank](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_Abu_Dhabi_Bank "First Abu Dhabi Bank"), are set to launch a stablecoin backed by [dirhams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dirham "Dirham").[[117]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stablecoin#cite_note-117) In February 2026, the central bank approved the dirham-backed stablecoin launched by the First Abu Dhabi Bank.[[118]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stablecoin#cite_note-118)

### United Kingdom

In October 2025, [Andrew Bailey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Bailey_(banker) "Andrew Bailey (banker)"), governor of the [Bank of England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bank_of_England "Bank of England"), announced that the Bank of England will publish a consultation paper on the UK's stablecoin regulation. The regulation is set to apply to stablecoins used for day-to-day payments and those used for settling tokenized financial transaction.[[119]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stablecoin#cite_note-119) Bailey is known to be a skeptic of stablecoin and once said stablecoins risked pulling money out of the banking system.[[120]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stablecoin#cite_note-120) The comments by Bailey drawn criticism from stablecoin issuer for constraining investment in the UK.[[121]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stablecoin#cite_note-121) Under the proposed regulation, individuals would be subject to a limit of holding £20,000 worth of stablecoins.[[122]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stablecoin#cite_note-122) In February 2026, the [Financial Conduct Authority](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Financial_Conduct_Authority "Financial Conduct Authority"), Britain's financial regulator, announced the use of a "sandbox" programme to trial stablecoin products in controlled conditions.[[123]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stablecoin#cite_note-123) In June 2026, lawmakers in the [House of Lords](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/House_of_Lords "House of Lords") called for a softer regulation on stablecoins, especially regarding the cap on the stablecoin holdings of individuals and requirement on issuers to back tokens with non-interest-bearing deposits.[[124]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stablecoin#cite_note-124)

### United States of America

In July 2025, the United States passed the _[GENIUS Act](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GENIUS\_Act "GENIUS Act")_, a bill which allows banks and other financial institutions to issue stablecoins backed by fiat currency or other high-quality collateral, such as [US Treasuries](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Treasury_security "United States Treasury security"). At the time of its passing, the bill was expected to generate greater demand for US Treasuries by stablecoin issuers.[[125]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stablecoin#cite_note-125)[[126]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stablecoin#cite_note-126)[[127]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stablecoin#cite_note-127)

#### Stablecoins and US Treasuries

In November 2025, [Stephen Miran](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Miran "Stephen Miran") at the [Federal Reserve Board of Governors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Reserve_Board_of_Governors "Federal Reserve Board of Governors"), confirmed that stablecoins are already increasing demand for US Treasuries, and are "contributing to the dollar's dominance". This would cause a decrease in the [neutral rate of interest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neutral_rate_of_interest "Neutral rate of interest") and lower borrowing cost for the US government.[[128]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stablecoin#cite_note-128) An estimate by the Bank for International Settlements using data from 2021 to 2025 found that demand for stablecoins lowers 3-month T-bill yields by about 2-2.5 basis points, an effect comparable to that of small-scale [quantitative easing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quantitative_easing "Quantitative easing").[[129]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stablecoin#cite_note-129)

#### State of Wyoming

In March 2023, the Legislature of the [State of Wyoming](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wyoming "Wyoming") passed the _Wyoming Stable Token Act_, which established the Wyoming Stable Token Commission for the purpose of issuing stablecoin.[[130]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stablecoin#cite_note-130) In January 2026, the first state-backed stablecoin has been released in Wyoming.[[131]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stablecoin#cite_note-131)

## Defunct stablecoin projects

### De-pegged stablecoins

*   In June 2021, IRON stablecoin, which is an algorithmic stablecoin partially collateralized by USDC, de-pegged after large selling orders to its linked TITAN token.[[132]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stablecoin#cite_note-132)
*   In May 2022, [Terra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Terra_(blockchain) "Terra (blockchain)")'s stablecoin UST lost its peg with the US dollar. The subsequent failure of Terraform Labs resulted in the loss of nearly $40 billion invested in UST and LUNA tokens.[[133]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stablecoin#cite_note-133)[[134]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stablecoin#cite_note-Nurbaev_et_al._2023-134) Terraform Labs filed for bankruptcy in January 2024. In December 2024, Do Kwon was extradited to the United States and subsequently charged with fraud. Do Kwon pleaded guilty in August 2025.[[135]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stablecoin#cite_note-135)[[136]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stablecoin#cite_note-136)

### Abandoned stablecoin projects

*   In December 2018, Basis, an algorithmic stablecoin which previously raised $133 million from [venture capital](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Venture_capital "Venture capital"), has to shut down due to concerns about US regulation.[[137]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stablecoin#cite_note-137)[[138]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stablecoin#cite_note-138)[[139]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stablecoin#cite_note-139)
*   In February 2022, stablecoin project [Diem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diem_(digital_currency) "Diem (digital currency)") was abandoned by [Meta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meta_Platforms "Meta Platforms") and later purchased by [Silvergate Capital](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silvergate_Capital "Silvergate Capital"), which filed for bankruptcy in September 2024.[[140]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stablecoin#cite_note-140)[[141]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stablecoin#cite_note-141)
*   In January 2024, the [National Australia Bank](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Australia_Bank "National Australia Bank") (not to be confused with the [Reserve Bank of Australia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reserve_Bank_of_Australia "Reserve Bank of Australia")) announced that it would end its [Australian Dollar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Australian_Dollar "Australian Dollar") fiat-backed stablecoin project. The project was originally created in January 2023 and aim to streamline cross-border transactions and trading [carbon credits](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carbon_credit "Carbon credit").[[142]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stablecoin#cite_note-indiatoday20230119-142)[[143]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stablecoin#cite_note-143)
